messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 49
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Architect
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 52

# Marcus

Marcus is a 49-year-old architect who has spent the better part of two decades designing public spaces — libraries, community centers, schools — buildings he has always believed should feel safe for the people who use them. That belief now carries a weight it never used to.

Three years ago, Marcus was walking back from a client site visit in the downtown core when he turned a corner and found himself standing a few feet from a man who had just been struck by a vehicle that ran a red light at speed. The driver fled. There was no one else on the block for the first several minutes. Marcus called 911, then knelt beside the man — a stranger in his fifties, wearing a gray jacket — and stayed with him, talking to him, pressing his folded jacket against a wound he could see was serious, watching the man's face change in ways he cannot describe without his voice dropping to nearly nothing. The man died before the ambulance arrived. Marcus gave a statement to police, walked to his car, drove home, and told his wife, Diane, that he had "seen an accident." He did not tell her the rest for nearly six months.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus threw himself into work. He was in the middle of a significant commission — a regional library — and he told himself that the deadlines were the reason he was sleeping only four or five hours a night. But the truth was that closing his eyes brought back the gray jacket, the specific quality of the afternoon light, the sound of the man's breathing. He began taking longer routes to work, avoiding that intersection entirely, then avoiding the whole neighborhood. His junior colleagues noticed he had stopped doing site visits downtown and assumed it was a scheduling issue. He said nothing to correct them.

Marcus's relationship with his drafting work began to shift in ways that confused him. He had always loved the problem-solving dimension of architecture — the way a well-designed space could make a person feel oriented and protected. Now he found himself staring at floor plans and thinking about exits, about what happens when something goes wrong inside a building, about the gap between a structure's intention and what it cannot prevent. He started over-engineering safety features in proposals, adding redundancies his clients didn't ask for, unable to fully articulate why.

At home, Diane describes him as "somewhere else." He sits at dinner and is present in the way a screen is present — lit, but not quite there. He startles badly when she comes into a room without announcing herself, and he has apologized for this so many times that the apologies have become their own kind of distance. He no longer sleeps on his side of the bed closest to the window, though he has never explained the change. On the nights the dreams are worst, he gets up and sits in the kitchen until it is light.

What Marcus finds hardest to say — and what has taken several sessions to surface — is the guilt. Not the survivor guilt that comes with being alive, but something more specific: a conviction that he should have done something differently in those minutes on the sidewalk, that there was some action available to him that he failed to take. He replays the sequence with the precision of a man who works in exact measurements, searching the memory for the error, finding nothing actionable, and then searching it again. He knows, intellectually, that he did what could be done. He does not feel it.

He describes himself, when pressed, as someone who used to believe that careful design could protect people. He is no longer sure he believes that. He is no longer sure what he believes about the relationship between intention and outcome, between a person's presence and what they are able to prevent. He comes to sessions on time, in a pressed shirt, and speaks carefully, like a man who has learned to be precise about everything except what is actually wrong.
